title: MATLAB and Octave
subtitle: The matrix language of science and engineering, taught through free GNU Octave, from a first script to linear algebra, ODEs, data analysis and a complete project.
description: MATLAB ("matrix laboratory") is a language and environment for numerical computing in which the basic value is a matrix. Engineers, scientists and students use it to solve linear systems, simulate differential equations, process signals and images, design control systems and analyse data, usually with a few lines of vectorised code where other languages would need loops. MATLAB is proprietary software from MathWorks, sold with many add-on toolboxes and the Simulink modelling environment. GNU Octave is a free, open-source program that runs most MATLAB code, and this course teaches the language through Octave, saying clearly wherever the two differ.

This course is for anyone who already knows what a variable, a loop and a function are: the Start level of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) or equivalent experience in any language. A little algebra helps; the linear algebra and calculus that appear are explained as they come. It covers matrices and indexing, vectorised arithmetic and control flow, scripts and functions, text, cell arrays and structs, solving linear systems, numerical methods (roots, integration and ODEs with ode45), data analysis and plotting, the toolbox and Simulink ecosystem, alternatives such as Python with NumPy and Julia, and a complete small project.

To run the code, install GNU Octave from [octave.org](https://octave.org/download) (Windows, macOS and Linux; it is free), or use MATLAB if you have a licence; MathWorks also offers MATLAB in the browser, [MATLAB Online](https://matlab.mathworks.com/), with a MathWorks account. Every complete program in these lessons was run with GNU Octave 11 by Lumenary's test suite, and the output shown is what Octave printed; MATLAB prints the same values but lays out automatic displays slightly differently. The lessons were drafted with AI assistance and are awaiting review by a human computer scientist.

levels.title: Foundations
levels.summary: Install Octave, run scripts, and learn the core of the language: matrices as the basic type, creating and indexing arrays, vectorised arithmetic and control flow.

levels.title: Practice
levels.summary: Organise code into scripts and functions with handles and error handling, work with text, cell arrays and structs, and solve linear systems the way numerical analysts do.

levels.title: Professional
levels.summary: Find roots, integrate and solve differential equations with the built-in solvers, analyse and plot data, know where toolboxes, Simulink, NumPy and Julia fit, and build a complete project.
